prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "SAP SE" (ticker SAP), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "SAP", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: SAP SE
result.industry: Enterprise application software (ERP and business cloud)
markets: Enterprise resource planning (ERP) and finance software
Procurement and spend management (Ariba, Concur, Fieldglass)
Supply chain management and manufacturing software
Business technology platform, data and analytics (BTP, Business Data Cloud)

mission.statement: Help the world run better and improve people's lives.
mission.source: SAP company website (purpose and strategy) and SAP Integrated Report
mission.plain: SAP wants companies to run smoothly with its software so that people's lives get better.

about.plain: SAP makes the software that big companies use to run themselves: to pay bills, pay staff, buy supplies, plan factories and keep track of orders. Think of it as the brain and record book of a company. More and more of it is rented over the internet (the cloud) instead of installed on the company's own computers. SAP is now adding AI helpers, called Joule, that can do some of this office work automatically.
about.customers: Mostly large and mid-sized companies and governments around the world, including most of the world's biggest firms.
about.everyday: When you buy a soda, a car or a pair of sneakers, there is a good chance the maker used SAP software to order parts, run the factory and pay its workers.

money.plain: renting SAP software over the internet, led by Cloud ERP Suite (€18.1B in 2025)
yearly maintenance fees on software customers installed themselves
consulting, training and help moving customers to the cloud
one-time sales of software to install on company computers (shrinking)
a data platform launched in 2025 that joins SAP and non-SAP data for analytics and AI
AI assistants and agents that do finance, HR and supply-chain work on their own

result.summary: SAP has a wide moat built mainly on switching costs: its ERP systems sit at the core of how thousands of the world's largest companies record money, people and goods, and replacing them takes years and huge risk. It also owns decades of industry process know-how and a large partner ecosystem. The main open question in 2026 is whether AI agents and new data platforms erode the value of the application layer, which has hit the share price even as cloud revenue keeps growing over 20%.

pricingPower.evidence: SAP has raised support fees and moved customers from maintenance to higher-priced RISE with SAP cloud contracts (cloud revenue rose from €8.7B in 2021 to €21.0B in 2025, +23% in 2025) while customers stayed; current cloud backlog was €22.9B at June 2026, up 27%, and the 2027 end of ECC mainstream support pushes migrations onto its pricing terms.

moats.evidence: SAP is the default name for ERP among large enterprises and CFOs ('nobody gets fired for buying SAP'), but its brand matters to business buyers, not consumers.

ERP holds a company's finance, payroll, inventory and processes; migrations take years and cost many times the license, so customers usually stay and move from ECC to S/4HANA rather than switch vendors.

A large ecosystem of system integrators (Accenture, Deloitte, IBM), hundreds of thousands of certified consultants and the SAP Business Network (Ariba) make SAP more useful the more firms and partners use it.

With €36.8B of 2025 revenue and €6.6B of R&D, SAP spreads development over a far larger base than most application rivals, though hyperscaler hosting costs keep cloud gross margins below pure SaaS peers.
The large-enterprise ERP market supports only a few full-suite vendors (SAP, Oracle, Microsoft, Infor), but it is not a natural monopoly.
SAP is the incumbent being challenged by cloud-native and AI-native vendors rather than the one counter-positioning against others.
Over 50 years SAP has encoded best-practice processes for 25+ industries, including complex tax, compliance and localisation rules for many countries, which is very hard for newcomers to replicate.
SAP holds the structured business data of many of the world's largest firms and controls access to it, which it argues is the key input for reliable business AI.

customers.evidence: Retention is very high because of switching costs and cloud backlog grew 25% in 2025, but satisfaction surveys (for example user groups such as DSAG and ASUG) often criticise cost, complexity and pressure to migrate to RISE before ECC support ends in 2027.

talent.evidence: SAP is a top employer brand in Germany for IT graduates and employed 110,650 people at end-2025 (37,965 in R&D), but the 2024 restructuring program (€3.1B charge) and job cuts dented morale.

product.evidence: S/4HANA and SAP Cloud ERP are widely regarded as the most complete large-enterprise ERP suite, regularly named a Leader in Gartner Magic Quadrants for cloud ERP, procurement and HCM, though Oracle Fusion and Workday often win in user-experience and cloud-native comparisons.

competitors.name: Oracle Corporation
competitors.note: Oracle Fusion Cloud ERP, NetSuite and HCM compete head-on for finance, supply chain and HR suites; Oracle also competes in databases.

competitors.name: Microsoft Corporation
competitors.note: Dynamics 365 Finance, Supply Chain and Business Central compete in mid-market and divisional ERP and CRM; Microsoft is also a key SAP cloud partner.

competitors.name: Workday, Inc.
competitors.note: Workday HCM and Financials compete with SuccessFactors and SAP finance in large enterprises.

competitors.name: Infor (Koch Industries)
competitors.note: Private industry-specific cloud ERP (CloudSuite) for manufacturing, distribution and healthcare.

competitors.name: Salesforce, Inc.
competitors.note: Competes with SAP Customer Experience (sales, service, commerce) and in AI agents (Agentforce).

competitors.name: ServiceNow, Inc.
competitors.note: Workflow and AI agent platform increasingly targeting HR, procurement and finance processes on top of ERP.

competitors.name: IFS
competitors.note: Private Swedish vendor of ERP, asset management and field service software for asset-intensive industries.

competitors.name: Epicor Software
competitors.note: Private (CD&R) mid-market ERP for manufacturers and distributors.

competitors.name: The Sage Group plc
competitors.note: Small and mid-sized business accounting and ERP (Sage Intacct, Sage X3) against SAP Business One and ByDesign.

competitors.name: UKG
competitors.note: Private HCM and payroll vendor competing with SuccessFactors.

competitors.name: Coupa Software
competitors.note: Private (Thoma Bravo) spend management platform competing with SAP Ariba and Concur.

competitors.name: Blue Yonder (Panasonic Holdings)
competitors.note: Supply chain planning and execution software competing with SAP IBP and EWM.

competitors.name: Manhattan Associates, Inc.
competitors.note: Warehouse, transportation and omnichannel supply chain execution software.

competitors.name: Kinaxis Inc.
competitors.note: Supply chain planning (RapidResponse/Maestro) competing with SAP IBP.

competitors.name: Databricks
competitors.note: Private data and AI platform; both partner and competitor to SAP Business Data Cloud for enterprise data.

threats: AI agents and AI-native vendors could shift value away from the application layer and seat-based pricing, the fear behind the roughly 30% fall in the share price from its 2025 peak.
Data platforms (Databricks, Snowflake, hyperscalers) and workflow layers (ServiceNow, Salesforce Agentforce) could sit on top of SAP and own the customer relationship.
Customers who resist RISE migration before ECC mainstream support ends in 2027 could choose third-party support (Rimini Street) or move to Oracle, Workday or Microsoft.
Slowing current cloud backlog growth (SAP guided to slight deceleration in 2026) would undercut the cloud transition story.
Regulatory scrutiny of maintenance and licensing practices; the EU closed its ERP support investigation in 2026 only after SAP gave binding commitments.
Dependence on hyperscalers (AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud) for hosting, which also compete for the AI and data layer.

ceo.name: Christian Klein
ceo.background: Business administration graduate of the University of Cooperative Education in Mannheim; joined SAP as a student in 1999, later COO; co-CEO from October 2019 and sole CEO since April 2020.

c1.evidence: SAP leads (with Oracle) the large-enterprise ERP market, which is mature, but its cloud ERP business is growing fast, with Cloud ERP Suite revenue up 25% in Q2 2026.

c2.evidence: Customers choose SAP for the most complete, industry-specific process suite and a huge partner ecosystem, and decades of encoded process know-how plus switching costs make that advantage hard to copy.

c3.evidence: SAP is the default ERP choice for large corporations, but most ordinary consumers do not know the name and user reviews often call it complex and expensive.

c4.evidence: SAP repeats its purpose to 'help the world run better and improve people's lives', but management messaging focuses mostly on cloud growth, margins and buybacks.

c6.evidence: “German, enterprise software, complex, expensive, reliable” — business users see SAP as solid and indispensable but bureaucratic and hard to implement, so the impression is mixed to mildly positive.

c7.evidence: Enterprise application software is a large market moving from on-premise to cloud and now to AI, and SAP's 2026 outlook is for 23-25% cloud revenue growth to €25.8-26.2B.

c8.evidence: SAP is expanding into data (Business Data Cloud, Dremio acquisition in 2026) and business AI agents (Joule), but these build on its existing enterprise customer base rather than opening entirely new markets.

m1.evidence: Christian Klein has a clear plan to move all customers to the cloud and build an 'Autonomous Enterprise' with business AI, but he is seen as an executor more than a visionary.

m2.evidence: Klein is a career SAP insider since 1999 who thinks long term about the cloud transition, but he is a professional manager, not a founder.

m4.evidence: There is no strong public evidence either way; the 2024 restructuring affecting about 10,000 roles drew employee criticism.

m5.evidence: Klein has pushed an engineering and AI-first culture, but SAP's culture is known as process-heavy and consensus-driven rather than inventive.

m6.evidence: Klein has a business administration background and rose through controlling and operations, though he is closely involved in the product roadmap and was SAP's COO.

m7.evidence: No controversies are known around Klein's character, but there is no clear evidence of stewardship aimed beyond SAP's business performance.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Christian Klein at a top university has been found.

m8b.evidence: Klein has a low-key, technocratic public persona, unlike celebrity founder CEOs.

m9.evidence: Under Klein, cloud revenue rose from €8.7B in 2021 to €21.0B in 2025 and IFRS operating profit reached €9.6B in 2025 with free cash flow of €8.2B, meeting or beating guidance.

m10.evidence: SAP cut costs through its 2024 restructuring program (€3.1B charge) to lift margins, but it is not known for a frugal culture.

c10.evidence: SAP software runs much of the world's business (payroll, supply chains, invoicing), helping billions indirectly, but end consumers rarely interact with it.

p2.evidence: Building a global ERP that handles accounting, tax and regulation for dozens of countries and industries is extremely hard and is core infrastructure for the world economy.

f1.evidence: Revenue from continuing operations rose every year from 2021 to 2025 (€26,953M to €36,800M); 2021 is only lower than 2020's €27,338M because 2021 was restated to exclude Qualtrics.

f2.evidence: Operating margin rose from 23.4% in 2021 to 26.1% in 2025, but gross margin was flat at about 73% (73.2% in 2021, 72.9% in 2025) as cloud mix rose.

f3.evidence: At end-2025 SAP had €8,220M cash plus €1,552M current financial assets against €8,071M financial liabilities, €8,239M free cash flow and €45,073M of equity.

f4.evidence: Operating profit fell from €6,308M (2021) to €4,665M (2024) due to restructuring and cloud transition costs, then jumped to €9,617M in 2025, with operating cash flow at a record €9,156M.

v1.evidence: SAP is the broadest ERP for large global companies, but Oracle, Workday and Microsoft are credible alternatives, so it is not clearly best in every case.

v2.evidence: SAP regularly ranks among Germany's most attractive employers for IT graduates, but 2024 restructuring hurt its reputation as an employer.

c5.evidence: If SAP disappeared, thousands of large companies would struggle to pay staff, ship goods and close their books, so businesses would miss it badly even though consumers would not notice directly.
